at.step: A hash join's build side is twenty times the memory budget. A textbook hash table cannot hold it, yet the join finishes, counting every row it must write to a temporary file before it is read back. Predict: with the budget at one twentieth of the build side, how many batches does the join need, what fraction of order rows goes to temporary files, and how many bits per customer does a runtime filter spend?

PostgreSQL's probe-side table chains tuples of any size in buckets sized for one tuple each on average. Spark's table for a single long-integer key is a different family entirely: open addressing, with quadratic probing and triangular numbers choosing the next slot, compact and cache-friendly because the key is one fixed-size number.

One 32-bit hash value answers two unrelated questions. Its low bits, masked against the bucket count, give the bucket inside the current batch. The same value, rotated right by the bucket count's log base two and masked against the batch count, gives the batch. Bucket and batch come from non-overlapping views of one hash.

The executor starts with one batch and doubles the count whenever a batch outgrows the memory budget. On the shop's instance, at a budget of one twentieth of the build side, doubling runs from one batch to thirty-two before every batch finally fits.

at.step: Before the join reads a single order, a Bloom filter built from the customers side, the side with a selective predicate, travels to the orders side's scan and drops any order whose customer cannot possibly match. The rule's own names: the customers side is the creation side, the orders side is the application side.

Spark's default filter spends 8,388,608 bits on 1,000,000 expected items: 8.4 bits per item. The same ratio, run through the engine's own formula, chooses six hash functions. A filter actually built at this ratio and probed with keys it never inserted measures a false-positive rate matching what the formula predicts for those six hash functions.

at.step: PostgreSQL watches for exactly this case: a split that leaves a batch keeping all, or none, of its tuples. When that happens the executor disables further growth in the number of batches globally, not only for that one batch, because the same key would defeat every later split just as it defeated this one.
